author: blu
body: `collate-key` answers a Text whose ENCODING order is collation order on the text it was built from. That is the whole design: it means `text-compare (collate-key a) (collate-key b)` is the collation of `a` and `b`, so a caller sorts by extracting one key per element and then comparing keys with the primitive it already had. No comparator type changes, and the rank tables below are consulted once per character per element rather than once per comparison.

author: blu
body: A key is two runs with a zero byte between them. The first run carries one primary weight per character, which is the script and the base letter with case and accent removed. The second carries the case and accent distinctions. Because the separator is lower than every weight, a primary difference anywhere decides the comparison before the second run is reached, and two texts that differ only in case or accent are separated by the second run alone.

author: blu
body: Beyond tier 0 every character takes one weight above all of these, so order falls back to encoding order within that group rather than pretending to a ranking this chapter does not have.

author: blu
body: The second run folds accent and case together. Nothing in the tree needs to tell an accent difference from a case difference, and a reader comparing two words wants one tie-break rather than two. An unaccented lowercase letter weighs 1, an uppercase letter 2, and each accented form takes its own weight above both so that a base letter sorts before every accented form of itself.

author: blu
body: For a one-off comparison, where building two keys and throwing them away costs less than the plumbing to keep them. A sort should extract keys once per element instead and compare those with `text-compare`.
